issue_context.title: Verify KestrelServerLimits are enforced for HTTP/3
issue_context.body:
We should have equivalents to most of [Http2TimeoutTests](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/6edcfe986a83274199feae1d8598cc8cd4f3b9ea/src/Servers/Kestrel/test/InMemory.FunctionalTests/Http2/Http2TimeoutTests.cs) for HTTP/3.

Timeouts to add and/or verify:
- [x] Min combined request body rate timeouts
  - [KestrelServerLimits.MinRequestBodyDataRate](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/c4d043dc86e52e8b83f8c0ef3500f2985f90c23c/src/Servers/Kestrel/Core/src/KestrelServerLimits.cs#L269-L280)
  - HTTP/3 should partially support the [IHttpMinRequestBodyDataRateFeature](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/c4d043dc86e52e8b83f8c0ef3500f2985f90c23c/src/Servers/Kestrel/Core/src/Features/IHttpMinRequestBodyDataRateFeature.cs).
  - Tracked individually by #29655
- [x] Min combined response rate timeouts
  - [KestrelServerLimits.MinResponseDataRate](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/c4d043dc86e52e8b83f8c0ef3500f2985f90c23c/src/Servers/Kestrel/Core/src/KestrelServerLimits.cs#L282-L304)
  - This is everything sent to the client. The response headers, response body, control frames, etc...
- [x] Response drain timeouts
  - Derived from [KestrelServerLimits.MinResponseDataRate](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/c4d043dc86e52e8b83f8c0ef3500f2985f90c23c/src/Servers/Kestrel/Core/src/KestrelServerLimits.cs#L282-L304) and [KestrelServerLimits.MaxResponseBufferSize](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/c4d043dc86e52e8b83f8c0ef3500f2985f90c23c/src/Servers/Kestrel/Core/src/KestrelServerLimits.cs#L45-L67)
  - When there's backpressure on the underlying stream/connection after `PipeWriter.FlushAsync()` completes which can happen with non-zero `PauseWriterThreshold`.
- [x] Request header timeouts
  - [KestrelServerLimits.RequestHeadersTimeout](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/c4d043dc86e52e8b83f8c0ef3500f2985f90c23c/src/Servers/Kestrel/Core/src/KestrelServerLimits.cs#L189-L206)
- [x] Keep-alive timeouts (will use msquic timeout)
  - [KestrelServerLimits.KeepAliveTimeout](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/c4d043dc86e52e8b83f8c0ef3500f2985f90c23c/src/Servers/Kestrel/Core/src/KestrelServerLimits.cs#L170-L187)
  - We probably don't want to keep idle QuicConnections around forever

If any the above bullet points aren't implemented yet, they probably deserve their own issue. The same goes for the size and count based limits in KestrelServerLimits:

- [x] MaxRequestLineSize
- [x] MaxRequestHeadersTotalSize
- [x] MaxRequestHeaderCount
- [x] MaxRequestBodySize (+IHttpMaxRequestBodySizeFeature)
- [x] MaxConcurrentConnections

re: RequestHeadersTimeout

~Decision is for now HTTP/3 won't use it. In HTTP/2 RequestHeadersTimeout is used as a timeout between receiving the HEADER frame and any CONTINUATION frames at the start of the request. In HTTP/3 the [HEADERS frame](https://quicwg.org/base-drafts/draft-ietf-quic-http.html#name-headers) always contains all HEADERS, so the timeout no longer has the same use in HTTP/3.~

Will use the timeout. Timeout starts before the request stream starts awaiting data and is canceled once HEADERS frame is received.

review_comments:
I agree. The problem is layering.

There needs to be a public API that the Quic transport and Kestrel share. There isn't an `IConnectionCompleteDrainFeature` unless we add one. This callback API gets the job done and already exists. There is a bit of overhead because the callback is registered, executed, and then immediately removed each time.

Ah, Http3StreamContext.StreamContext is a ConnectionContext, not a QuicStreamContext, so the caller wouldn't have access to any new API unless we added it to the base type. Given this usage pattern that still might be worth considering. Is adding one new virtual method on the base type better than a callback pattern?

Do you anticipate other uses for the IConnectionCompleteFeature?

I doubt it.

IMO we can leave adding a new feature, or method, to after .NET 6.

This scares me considering DisposeAsync() pools. Does this mean something could still have a reference to the QuicStreamContext and dispose it after pooling? Maybe we should move the pooling logic outside of DisposeAsync since this is exposed to connection middleware and DisposeAsync() can be called multiple times.

I added that when I was considering a design that wasn't as safe. I quickly decided that it wasn't a good idea. This was leftover from the first attempt. Do you want it removed?

When a QUIC stream is disposed of the callback removes it from the connection before it is pooled. And only gracefully completed requests are pooled. No active request will be using a pooled stream.
What happens if connection middleware disposes the ConnectionContext before exiting?

If the app (which is Kestrel HTTP/3 implementation in this case) hasn't completed the pipes then it isn't pooled.

https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/a079651ab7bfe2c086ab26567c12364f0a4f2480/src/Servers/Kestrel/Transport.Quic/src/Internal/QuicStreamContext.cs#L418-L422

But third-party middleware could complete the Pipes, right? Sorry to randomize this PR. I do not think the pooling logic needs to be reworked before merging this. And I'll admit this likely isn't the most likely scenario. It's just seeing this got me thinking about pooling too early, and if it *did* become a problem, it might be very hard to diagnose.

Yes.

There has to be some public API and condition at which point the context is pooled. Whatever we use, there is the ability for someone to use the public API to trigger pooling early.
